etymology: From the plain English of the Authorized Version, rendering the Hebrew of 1 Samuel 17:40; the stones David chose from the brook to face the giant of Gath.
biblical_def: The five smooth stones are the weapons David chose from the brook when he went down to meet Goliath, refusing the armour of Saul and trusting the LORD of hosts. The text records that he took his staff, chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, put them in a shepherd's bag, and with his sling in his hand drew near to the Philistine. The phrase has become a byword for the simple, despised instrument through which God overthrows the proud, for David himself declared that the battle is the LORD'S, who saveth not with sword and spear. The dictionary reads the stones in the line of the apostle: God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty, and the weapons of our warfare are not carnal but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds. Whether the four unused stones point to Goliath's four giant kinsmen, as some have observed, or simply mark a prudent provision, the great lesson stands: faith does not despise means, for David stooped to gather the stones, yet faith does not trust in means, for the victory is God's alone. The five smooth stones rebuke both the presumption that waits for miracle without effort and the carnal confidence that trusts the sling rather than the LORD who guides it.
webster_summary: The stones David chose from the brook to face Goliath; a byword for the simple, despised means through which God confounds the mighty, neither despising means nor trusting in them.
webster_full: FIVE SMOOTH STONES, noun phrase. The stones David chose from the brook to slay Goliath (1 Samuel 17:40).
He refused Saul's armour and took sling and stones, declaring the battle to be the LORD'S.
A single stone smote the giant in the forehead and felled him.
Figuratively, the weak and despised instrument by which God overthrows the proud and mighty.
An emblem of faith that uses means without trusting in them, for the victory is of the LORD.
scriptures: And he took his staff in his hand, and chose him five smooth stones out of the brook, and put them in a shepherd's bag which he had, even in a scrip; and his sling was in his hand: and he drew near to the Philistine.
And all this assembly shall know that the LORD saveth not with sword and spear: for the battle is the LORD'S, and he will give you into our hands.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
corruption_summary: Severed from the LORD of the battle, the phrase becomes a motivational emblem of human pluck, as though the stones, not God, won the day.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular use of “five smooth stones” has drifted into a slogan of self-reliance and clever underdog strategy, a cousin of the secularized David-and-Goliath trope. The dictionary refuses the drift. David gathered stones, but he conquered by the name of the LORD of hosts; the sling was in his hand, but the battle was the LORD'S. To make the stones the hero is to silence the very confession David shouted across the valley.

The recovery is the biblical balance between means and faith. Faith is not idleness: David stooped to the brook and chose his stones with a shepherd's skill. Yet faith is not carnal confidence either: the apostle teaches that the weapons of our warfare are mighty not in themselves but through God. So the believer labours with the ordinary means God appoints—word, prayer, diligence—while trusting wholly in the LORD who alone gives the victory.
roots_summary: From the simple narrative Hebrew of 1 Samuel 17; “smooth” (Hebrew chalaq) marks the stones fit for the sling, gathered from the watercourse of the valley of Elah.
roots_lines: 'Eben, Hebrew, a stone, the ordinary word for the missiles of the sling.
Chalaq, Hebrew, smooth, the quality that made the brook-stones fit to fly true.
Nachal, Hebrew, the brook or wadi of the valley of Elah from which they were drawn.
The shepherd's “scrip” or bag marks David's lowly calling, despised by the giant.
The apostolic theme of weak things confounding the mighty (1 Corinthians 1:27) frames their meaning.
usage: The pastor warned against preaching the five smooth stones as a lesson in self-confidence, for David trusted the LORD and not the sling.
He gathered his “five smooth stones” of study and prayer, then cast himself wholly on God for the outcome.
She learned from the brook of Elah that faith uses means diligently yet trusts only the LORD of the battle.

etymology: From the Authorized Version rendering of the Hebrew rekeb 'esh, “chariot of fire”; the heavenly conveyance and host seen by Elijah and Elisha.
biblical_def: The chariots of fire are the heavenly host and conveyance revealed twice in the Elijah-Elisha narratives, the visible token of the unseen armies of the LORD that surround and serve His people. As Elijah and Elisha walked and talked, a chariot of fire and horses of fire parted them asunder, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven—not by death but by translation, so that Elisha cried, “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof.” Again, when the Syrian host compassed Dothan and Elisha's servant despaired, the prophet prayed that the young man's eyes be opened, and he saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha. The lesson Elisha drew is the dictionary's standard: “Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.” The chariots of fire teach the reality of the angelic host and the watchful providence of God, who maketh the chariots of His armies twenty thousand, even thousands of angels. They rebuke the unbelief that counts only the visible enemy and forgets the invisible defence. The believer's safety is not in the count of armies he can see but in the LORD of hosts whose burning chariots encamp round about them that fear Him.
webster_summary: The heavenly host and conveyance of fire seen at Elijah's translation and around Elisha at Dothan; a token of the angelic armies of the LORD that surround His people, more than all the foes they can see.
webster_full: CHARIOTS OF FIRE, noun phrase. [Hebrew rekeb 'esh.] The fiery host and chariot of the heavenly armies of the LORD.
A chariot and horses of fire parted Elijah from Elisha as Elijah was taken up by a whirlwind into heaven.
At Dothan the LORD opened the servant's eyes to see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire about Elisha.
Elisha confessed that they with him were more than they against him.
An emblem of the angelic host and the watchful providence that defends the people of God.
scriptures: And it came to pass, as they still went on, and talked, that, behold, there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
And he answered, Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.

And Elisha prayed, and said, LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha.
The chariots of God are twenty thousand, even thousands of angels: the Lord is among them, as in Sinai, in the holy place.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the practical unbelief that counts only the visible enemy and forgets the invisible host of God.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reality of the angelic host and the watchful providence it serves. The modern habit, even among believers, is to reckon the odds by what the eye can number—the Syrian army on the hill, the troubles that compass the soul—and to despair as Elisha's servant despaired. But the prophet's prayer is the believer's comfort: “LORD, open his eyes.” The chariots of fire were there before they were seen.

Scripture does not invite a morbid fascination with angels, nor the veneration of them that the apostle forbids (Colossians 2:18). It teaches their reality and their ministry: they are sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation (Hebrews 1:14). The dictionary holds the sober ground—neither denying the host nor worshipping it—and rests the believer's confidence not in counting angels but in the LORD of hosts who commands them, whose chariots are twenty thousand and who is Himself among them.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew rekeb (chariot) and 'esh (fire); the fire marks the host as heavenly and the presence as divine, as the fire of Sinai and the pillar by night.
roots_lines: Rekeb, Hebrew, a chariot or the body of chariotry of an army.
'Esh, Hebrew, fire, the recurring sign of the divine presence and the heavenly.
Sus 'esh, “horses of fire,” the steeds of the heavenly chariotry.
The whirlwind (Hebrew se'arah) bore Elijah up, a translation without death.
Elisha's cry, “the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof,” names the prophet as the true defence of the nation.
usage: When the threat seemed overwhelming, the elder read Dothan and prayed the LORD would open the people's eyes.
“They that be with us are more than they that be with them,” she repeated, counting the unseen host of God.
The pastor preached the chariots of fire to teach that providence guards the saints with armies the eye cannot number.

etymology: From the Authorized Version; Dan being the northernmost and Beersheba the southernmost settlement of the land, the phrase names the whole extent of Israel from end to end.
biblical_def: “From Dan to Beersheba” is the recurring biblical idiom for the whole land of Israel from its northern to its southern bound, as one might say “from one end of the country to the other.” Dan lay at the far north, near the springs of Jordan; Beersheba marked the southern edge toward the wilderness of the Negeb. When all Israel gathered as one man, the congregation came from Dan even to Beersheba; when Samuel was established a prophet, all Israel from Dan to Beersheba knew it; and when David sinned in numbering the people, Joab went through all the tribes from Dan even to Beersheba. The phrase carries more than geography. It marks the unity of the covenant people—all the tribes as one congregation before the LORD—and the breadth of His dealings, whether in blessing, when Judah and Israel dwelt safely under vine and fig tree throughout that whole compass in the days of Solomon, or in chastisement, when the numbering brought plague upon the same expanse. The dictionary marks the idiom as a witness to the corporate reality of the people of God: not a collection of scattered individuals but one nation under one LORD, gathered from end to end, accountable as one and blessed as one. The New Testament Israel of God, the church, is likewise one body, gathered out of every tribe and tongue from the ends of the earth.
webster_summary: The idiom for the whole land of Israel from its northern bound (Dan) to its southern (Beersheba); a witness to the corporate unity of the covenant people gathered as one congregation before the LORD.
webster_full: FROM DAN TO BEERSHEBA, idiomatic phrase. From the northernmost to the southernmost town of Israel; the whole extent of the land.
Used when all the tribes gathered as one man before the LORD (Judges 20:1).
Used of the universal knowledge that Samuel was a true prophet (1 Samuel 3:20).
Used of David's sinful numbering of the whole people (2 Samuel 24:2).
Figuratively, the corporate unity and full compass of the covenant people of God.
scriptures: Jud 20:1
Then all the children of Israel went out, and the congregation was gathered together as one man, from Dan even to Beersheba, with the land of Gilead, unto the LORD in Mizpeh.
And all Israel from Dan even to Beersheba knew that Samuel was established to be a prophet of the LORD.

For the king said to Joab the captain of the host, which was with him, Go now through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan even to Beersheba, and number ye the people, that I may know the number of the people.
And Judah and Israel dwelt safely, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, from Dan even to Beersheba, all the days of Solomon.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the individualism that forgets the corporate, covenantal reality the phrase declares.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the corporate solidarity of the people of God. The modern Western reading of Scripture is relentlessly individualistic, hearing every promise and warning as addressed to the solitary soul. “From Dan to Beersheba” resists that reading. Israel gathered as one man; Israel was blessed as one; Israel was numbered, and chastised, as one. The covenant is made with a people, and the individual stands within the people, not apart from it.

This is not collectivism, which dissolves the person into the mass, but covenant solidarity, in which real persons are bound together under one Head and one LORD. The same truth carries into the New Testament: the church is one body, gathered from the ends of the earth, members one of another (Romans 12:5). The dictionary recovers the corporate dimension the phrase teaches without losing the personal—each soul accountable, yet none isolated, for the LORD deals with His people from Dan to Beersheba as one.
roots_summary: From the place-names Dan (the northern limit) and Beersheba (the southern), bracketing the land; the merism names the whole by its two extremes.
roots_lines: Dan, the northernmost city, near the headwaters of Jordan, named for the tribe that settled there.
Be'er-sheva, Hebrew, “well of the oath” or “well of seven,” the southern town of Abraham and Isaac.
The figure is a merism, naming the whole (all the land) by its two outermost points.
Qahal, Hebrew, the congregation or assembly that gathered “as one man” across that compass.
The later reversal “from Beersheba to Dan” in Chronicles names the same whole from the southern viewpoint of Judah.
usage: The preacher used “from Dan to Beersheba” to show that the covenant binds a whole people, not a scattering of individuals.
He reminded the flock that Israel was numbered as one and chastised as one, from end to end of the land.
She saw in the gathered congregation “as one man” a pattern of the one body the church is meant to be.

etymology: From the Authorized Version rendering of the Hebrew dabaq, “to cleave, cling, pursue closely”; the soul's ardent pursuit of God in Psalm 63.
biblical_def: “My soul followeth hard after thee” is the cry of David in the wilderness of Judah, longing for God as in a dry and thirsty land where no water is. The Hebrew word rendered “followeth hard” is dabaq, the very word used of a man cleaving to his wife and of one clinging fast to another; it pictures not a casual seeking but a pressing, clinging pursuit that will not let go. The phrase names the holy ardour that ought to mark the believer's walk: a soul that thirsts for God, that follows close upon Him, that presses toward the mark, as the apostle says, for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus. It is the spirit of Caleb, who followed the LORD fully and had another spirit with him, and the spirit of Jacob, who would not let the Angel go except He blessed him. Yet the same verse guards against a false notion of this pursuit, for David adds at once, “thy right hand upholdeth me.” The soul follows hard after God only because God upholds the soul; the cleaving is real and active, yet it rests upon a prior grace. The dictionary marks the phrase as the answer both to spiritual sloth, which seeks God faintly if at all, and to a proud self-effort that forgets the upholding hand; true pursuit of God is ardent and wholehearted, and wholly dependent on the grace that draws it.
webster_summary: David's cry that his soul cleaves and presses close after God (Psalm 63:8); the holy ardour of wholehearted pursuit of the LORD, itself upheld by His sustaining grace.
webster_full: FOLLOW HARD AFTER, verb phrase. [Hebrew dabaq, to cleave or cling closely.] To pursue God with clinging, pressing ardour.
David's soul followed hard after God in the wilderness, thirsting for Him as for water.
The same word describes a man cleaving to his wife and the saint clinging to the LORD.
It answers to the apostle's pressing toward the mark (Philippians 3:14) and to Caleb's following the LORD fully.
The pursuit is upheld by God's right hand, an active cleaving that rests upon prior grace.
scriptures: My soul followeth hard after thee: thy right hand upholdeth me.
Php 3:14
I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.
But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully, him will I bring into the land whereinto he went; and his seed shall possess it.
As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God.
corruption_summary: The phrase is corrupted when ardent pursuit of God is collapsed either into a lazy “letting go and letting God” or into a striving that forgets the upholding hand of grace.
corruption_paragraphs: A strain of modern piety, reacting against works-righteousness, has made all active pursuit of God suspect, urging believers to cease striving and merely rest. But David did not rest passively; his soul followed hard after God, cleaving and pressing as a man cleaves to his bride. The dictionary names the quietist error: Scripture commands an ardent, wholehearted seeking of the Lord, and the gospel of grace does not abolish the pursuit but fuels it.

The opposite error is the proud self-effort that follows hard after God as though the cleaving were its own achievement. Against this David sets the second half of his verse: “thy right hand upholdeth me.” The soul cleaves because it is held; the pursuit is real and strenuous, and it rests wholly upon the prior and upholding grace of God. So Paul, who pressed toward the mark, could say in the same breath, “I laboured… yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10). True pursuit is ardent and dependent at once.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew dabaq, to cleave, cling, or follow hard; the same word for marital union (Genesis 2:24) and for clinging to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20).
roots_lines: Dabaq, Hebrew, to cleave, cling, adhere, or pursue closely.
The same verb in Genesis 2:24 describes a man cleaving to his wife.
In Deuteronomy 10:20 the people are commanded to cleave (dabaq) unto the LORD.
The Greek dioko in Philippians 3:14, “I press,” carries the same note of strenuous pursuit.
The upholding “right hand” (Hebrew yamin) grounds the pursuit in sustaining grace.
usage: The pastor urged the young believers to follow hard after God, not to rest in a passive piety that seeks Him faintly.
She marked that David's clinging was upheld by God's right hand, lest she trust her own pursuit.
He preached Caleb's “another spirit” as the picture of a soul that follows the LORD fully.

etymology: From the biblical theme of hating evil for God's sake; the “perfect hatred” of Psalm 139:22, set against the world's reduction of all hatred to sin.
biblical_def: Holy hatred is the settled abhorrence of evil that necessarily accompanies the love of God, named in Scripture as a duty and a mark of the godly. “Ye that love the LORD, hate evil,” says the psalmist; and the fear of the LORD is itself defined as hating evil—pride, arrogancy, the evil way, and the froward mouth. David, the man after God's own heart, could pray, “Do not I hate them, O LORD, that hate thee?… I hate them with perfect hatred: I count them mine enemies,” and the apostle commands the same affection in the New Testament: “Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.” This hatred is “holy” and “perfect” precisely because it is the negative side of love for God: he who truly loves the good must hate its destroyer, as a man who loves his children hates the disease that threatens them. It is not the carnal hatred the New Testament forbids—the malice, bitterness, and personal vengeance that spring from the fallen heart—for the same Scripture commands love of enemies and forbids private revenge. The dictionary marks holy hatred against two corruptions: the sentimental age that has made all hatred a sin and emptied love of its backbone, and the carnal counterfeit that baptizes private malice as zeal. True holy hatred hates the sin while loving the sinner, hates the evil for God's sake, and leaves vengeance to the LORD.
webster_summary: The settled abhorrence of evil that is the necessary other side of the love of God; commanded in Scripture, distinct alike from the sentimentality that forbids all hatred and the carnal malice that baptizes private revenge.
webster_full: HOLY HATRED, noun phrase. The God-honouring abhorrence of evil that accompanies true love of the good.
Commanded: “Ye that love the LORD, hate evil” (Psalm 97:10).
The fear of the LORD is defined as hating evil (Proverbs 8:13).
David's “perfect hatred” (Psalm 139:22) is zeal for God, not personal malice.
Distinct from carnal hatred, malice, and private vengeance, which Scripture forbids.
scriptures: Ye that love the LORD, hate evil: he preserveth the souls of his saints; he delivereth them out of the hand of the wicked.
I hate them with perfect hatred: I count them mine enemies.
The fear of the LORD is to hate evil: pride, and arrogancy, and the evil way, and the froward mouth, do I hate.
Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.
corruption_summary: The sentimental age has made all hatred a sin and emptied love of its backbone; the carnal counterfeit, on the other side, baptizes private malice and vengeance as godly zeal.
corruption_paragraphs: Therapy-culture and the sentimental gospel of the age have taught that love and hatred are simple opposites, so that to hate anything at all is to fail at love. This dissolves the biblical concept. Scripture commands the saint to hate evil precisely because he loves God; love that cannot hate what destroys its object is not love but indifference. The dictionary recovers holy hatred as the indispensable backbone of love: God Himself hates the wicked's way (Psalm 5:5; 11:5), and the godly hate evil for His sake.

The opposite corruption is older and uglier: the carnal heart that calls its own malice, grudges, and lust for revenge “righteous indignation.” Scripture forbids this with equal force—love your enemies, bless them that curse you, avenge not yourselves but give place unto wrath, for vengeance belongeth to the LORD. Holy hatred hates the sin and the evil way, loves the sinner enough to warn him, and leaves all retribution to the righteous Judge. The line is fine but firm: zeal for God against evil is commanded; private bitterness against persons is sin.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew sane' (to hate) used of the godly hating evil, and the Greek apostygeo (to abhor) in Romans 12:9; the “perfect” (Hebrew takhlith, completeness) hatred of David is zeal brought to its full.
roots_lines: Sane', Hebrew, to hate, used both of sinful malice and of holy abhorrence of evil.
Takhlith, Hebrew, completeness or perfection, the “perfect hatred” of Psalm 139:22.
Apostygeo, Greek, to abhor or shrink from with horror, in Romans 12:9.
The fear of the LORD is defined as hating evil (Proverbs 8:13), binding reverence to abhorrence.
The forbidden carnal hatred (Greek misos, malice) is distinguished by its object and its spirit.
usage: The preacher taught that a love which cannot hate evil is not love at all, but indifference dressed as kindness.
He warned the zealous young man that holy hatred hates the sin and pities the sinner, leaving vengeance to God.
She prayed David's “perfect hatred” of evil while begging grace to love the very people enslaved by it.

etymology: From the Authorized Version rendering of the Hebrew shebet barzel (Psalm 2:9) and the Greek rhabdos sidera (Revelation); the unbreakable sceptre of the Messiah's rule.
biblical_def: The rod of iron is the figure of the unbreakable, irresistible rule of the Messiah over the nations, given Him by the Father as the kingly inheritance of the Son. In the second Psalm the LORD declares concerning His Anointed, “Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel,” promising the raging nations and their kings either submission or shattering. The Revelation takes up the image three times: the man child caught up to God's throne is to rule all nations with a rod of iron; the overcomer is promised a share in that rule; and the rider on the white horse, called Faithful and True, smites the nations and rules them with a rod of iron, treading the winepress of the wrath of Almighty God. The figure binds two truths the dictionary holds: Christ reigns now, having received all authority in heaven and earth, and Christ shall come to judge, dashing in pieces every power that will not bow. The rod is of iron, not of reed; His kingdom cannot be broken, and those who set themselves against the LORD and His Anointed are not negotiated with but shattered like a potter's clay. The proper response is the Psalm's own counsel: “Kiss the Son, lest he be angry… Blessed are all they that put their trust in him.”
webster_summary: The figure of the unbreakable, irresistible rule of the Messiah over the nations (Psalm 2:9; Revelation 19:15); a sceptre of iron that either subdues or shatters every power set against the LORD and His Anointed.
webster_full: ROD OF IRON, noun phrase. [Hebrew shebet barzel.] The unbreakable sceptre of the Messiah's rule over the nations.
In Psalm 2:9 the Son breaks the raging nations as a potter's vessel.
In Revelation the man child and the overcomer share the rule with a rod of iron.
The rider Faithful and True smites the nations and rules them with a rod of iron (Revelation 19:15).
An emblem of a kingdom that cannot be broken and a judgment that shatters every rebel power.
scriptures: Ps 2:9
Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel.
And he shall rule them with a rod of iron; as the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers: even as I received of my Father.
And she brought forth a man child, who was to rule all nations with a rod of iron: and her child was caught up unto God, and to his throne.

And out of his mouth goeth a sharp sword, that with it he should smite the nations: and he shall rule them with a rod of iron: and he treadeth the winepress of the fierceness and wrath of Almighty God.
corruption_summary: The sentimental gospel cannot abide a Christ who shatters His enemies, and so quietly drops the rod of iron, leaving a Saviour who saves but never reigns in judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern preaching has so emphasized the meekness of Christ that it has lost His majesty, presenting a Saviour who only invites and never judges. The rod of iron rebukes this truncation. The same Lamb who was slain is the Lion who rules, and the Father has given Him the nations as His inheritance and the uttermost parts of the earth as His possession, to be ruled or shattered. To preach a Christ without the rod of iron is to preach half a Christ, and to flatter the raging nations that there is no day of reckoning.

The figure also corrects a false militancy among men, who would seize the iron rod for themselves and shatter their enemies in Christ's name. But the rod is the Son's, received of the Father; the overcomer shares it only by union with Him and at His appointing, not by the sword of the flesh. The dictionary holds the balance: Christ reigns now and will judge in righteousness, dashing every rebel power; and His people wait for that day, kissing the Son and trusting in Him, not avenging themselves but committing all to the King whose sceptre is iron and whose judgment is sure.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew shebet (rod, sceptre, tribe) and barzel (iron), with the Greek rhabdos sidera; iron marks the sceptre as unbreakable and the rule as irresistible.
roots_lines: Shebet, Hebrew, a rod, staff, or sceptre, also the word for a tribe.
Barzel, Hebrew, iron, marking the rod as unbreakable.
Rhabdos sidera, Greek, “iron rod,” the Septuagint and Revelation rendering.
The “potter's vessel” dashed in pieces (Psalm 2:9) figures the brittleness of rebel powers before the King.
The “winepress” of Revelation 19:15 binds the rod to the day of wrath.
usage: The pastor preached the rod of iron to recover the majesty of a Christ who not only saves but reigns and judges.
He warned the angry brother that the iron rod is the Son's, not ours, and vengeance belongs to the King.
She read Psalm 2 and learned to kiss the Son, putting her trust in the King whose kingdom cannot be broken.

etymology: From the Old English “dayspring,” the dawn or rising of the day, rendering the Greek anatole, the rising of the sun; a title of Christ in the song of Zacharias.
biblical_def: The dayspring from on high is a title of the Lord Jesus Christ taken from the prophecy of Zacharias, father of John the Baptist, who sang by the Spirit that “through the tender mercy of our God… the dayspring from on high hath visited us, to give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.” “Dayspring” is the dawn, the first rising of the light; the Greek anatole means the rising of the sun, and is the Septuagint word in the Branch prophecies, so that the title gathers up both the dawning Light and the messianic Branch. The image draws on Malachi's promise that the Sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in His wings, and on Isaiah's great people that walked in darkness seeing a great light. The dictionary marks the title as a confession of the incarnation: the Light did not rise from below, from man's striving or the religions of the earth, but visited us from on high, the heavenly dawn breaking upon a world sitting in the shadow of death. It is “through the tender mercy of our God” alone—not human merit—that the dawn came. As the morning star arises in the believer's heart, so Christ the dayspring scatters the darkness of sin and ignorance and guides the feet of His people into the way of peace, which is reconciliation with God.
webster_summary: A title of Christ from the song of Zacharias (Luke 1:78), the dawning Light from heaven who visits a world in the shadow of death; gathering up Malachi's Sun of righteousness and the messianic Branch.
webster_full: DAYSPRING FROM ON HIGH, noun phrase. [Greek anatole, the rising of the sun.] A title of Christ as the dawning Light from heaven.
From the song of Zacharias: the dayspring hath visited us through the tender mercy of God (Luke 1:78).
It gives light to them that sit in darkness and the shadow of death, and guides the feet into peace.
It gathers up Malachi's Sun of righteousness with healing in His wings (Malachi 4:2).
A confession of the incarnation: the Light rose not from man but visited us from on high.
scriptures: Through the tender mercy of our God; whereby the dayspring from on high hath visited us,
To give light to them that sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, to guide our feet into the way of peace.
Mal 4:2
But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the inner-light spirituality that locates the dawn in man's own soul rather than in the Christ who visits from on high.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the heavenly source of the light. Much modern spirituality, from Quaker inner-light to the therapeutic gospel of self-discovery, locates the dawn within—a divine spark, an inner wisdom, a true self to be uncovered. Zacharias confesses the opposite: the dayspring visited us from on high. Fallen man sits in darkness and the shadow of death; he does not generate the dawn but is visited by it, through the tender mercy of God and not by his own searching.

The title also guards the freeness of grace. The dawn came “through the tender mercy of our God,” not because the world had earned the light or sought it well. The same sovereign mercy that breaks the natural day upon the just and the unjust broke the Light of the world upon a people in darkness. The dictionary recovers the dayspring as a confession of the incarnation and of grace: Christ the rising Sun, come down from heaven, scattering the darkness no human candle could pierce and guiding His people into the way of peace with God.
roots_summary: From the Greek anatole (a rising, the east, the dawn), the Septuagint word for the messianic Branch; with the Old English “dayspring,” the springing-up of the day.
roots_lines: Anatole, Greek, the rising of the sun, the east, also “the Branch” in the Greek of Jeremiah and Zechariah.
“Dayspring,” Old English, the dawn or daybreak, the springing-up of the light.
Episkeptomai, Greek, “hath visited,” the verb of God's gracious coming to His people.
Malachi's “Sun of righteousness” (Hebrew shemesh tsedaqah) lies behind the figure.
The “day star” of 2 Peter 1:19 (Greek phosphoros) names Christ rising in the heart.
usage: At dawn services the church sang of the dayspring from on high, the Light that visited a world in the shadow of death.
He preached that the dawn came from heaven, not from within, rebuking the gospel of the inner light.
She took comfort that the dayspring visited us through tender mercy, and not for any worth in us.

etymology: From the Authorized Version; the “just” (righteous) balances, weights, ephah, and hin commanded in the law as the standard of honest dealing.
biblical_def: Just weights and measures are the biblical standard of honesty in commerce, commanded in the law and praised in the wisdom literature as the delight of the LORD. In the days of the balance and the measuring vessel, a merchant could cheat by carrying two sets of weights—a heavy one for buying and a light one for selling—or by shaving the ephah and the hin. The law forbids it utterly: “Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have,” and grounds the command in the character and redemption of God: “I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt.” The wisdom of Proverbs makes the point sharper still: a false balance is abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is His delight; divers weights and divers measures are alike an abomination. The dictionary marks this as the everyday outworking of the eighth and ninth commandments—thou shalt not steal, and thou shalt not bear false witness—in the marketplace, where so much religion is exposed as hollow. Honesty in the smallest transaction is no minor virtue; it is the test of whether the fear of God reaches the scales and the till. The principle reaches every modern equivalent: the contract, the invoice, the advertisement, the day's labour for the day's wage. A people that fears God keeps just weights, for the God who redeemed them is Himself the standard of perfect equity, and He weighs the weights of the merchant in the balances of His justice.
webster_summary: The biblical standard of honesty in commerce—true balances, weights, and measures—commanded in the law and called the LORD's delight; the everyday outworking of the commands against theft and false witness.
webster_full: JUST WEIGHTS AND MEASURES, noun phrase. True and honest balances, weights, and measuring vessels in trade.
Commanded in the law: just balances, just weights, a just ephah and hin (Leviticus 19:36).
A false balance is abomination to the LORD; a just weight is His delight (Proverbs 11:1).
Divers weights and divers measures are alike an abomination (Proverbs 20:10).
The marketplace test of the eighth and ninth commandments, and of the fear of God.
scriptures: Just balances, just weights, a just ephah, and a just hin, shall ye have: I am the LORD your God, which brought you out of the land of Egypt.
A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.
Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD.
But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have: that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the live corruption is the modern severing of private faith from public dealing, as though honesty in trade were no part of religion.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the lordship of Christ over commerce. A common error treats faith as a private and inward thing while business runs by its own rules of advantage; the man is devout on Sunday and shaves the ephah on Monday. Scripture knows no such division. The God who commands just weights is the God who redeemed His people, and He calls a false balance an abomination. The fear of God either reaches the scales or it is not the fear of God.

The principle translates directly into every modern instrument of exchange: the contract written to deceive, the invoice padded, the advertisement that lies, the hidden fee, the shoddy work billed as sound, the wage withheld. All are the divers weights and divers measures the LORD abhors. The dictionary recovers commercial honesty as a matter of true religion, for the same hand that weighs the merchant's gold is weighed itself in the balances of Him who keeps perfect equity and lengthens the days of the honest in the land.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew tsedeq (just, righteous) qualifying the balances and weights; the ephah (a dry measure) and hin (a liquid measure) are the standard vessels of trade.
roots_lines: Tsedeq, Hebrew, righteousness or justness, the word applied to balances, weights, and measures.
'Eben, Hebrew, a stone, used as the standard weight in the balance.
'Ephah, a dry measure of about a bushel; hin, a liquid measure, both to be “just.”
“Divers weights” (Hebrew 'eben va'eben, “a stone and a stone”) names the two-weight fraud.
The command rests on the eighth (theft) and ninth (false witness) words of the Decalogue.
usage: The elder taught the tradesmen that just weights are true religion, and a padded invoice is an abomination to the LORD.
He refused the deceptive contract, remembering that divers measures are alike hateful to God.
She reminded her sons that the God who redeemed them weighs the merchant's scales in the balances of His justice.

etymology: From the Latin peculium, private property or treasure, rendering the Hebrew segullah (a treasured possession) and the Greek peripoiesis; God's own treasured people.
biblical_def: “Peculiar people” is the Authorized Version's rendering of the great covenant title by which God names His redeemed as His own treasured possession, set apart from all nations to be His. The English word, drawn from the Latin peculium, did not originally mean “odd” but “belonging exclusively to one—one's private treasure.” So Peter gathers up the titles of Israel and lays them upon the church: “Ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light.” Paul says the same: Christ gave Himself to purify unto Himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works. The roots run back to Sinai, where the LORD promised that if Israel kept His covenant they should be a peculiar treasure unto Him above all people, and to Deuteronomy, where He chose them to be a peculiar people unto Himself. The dictionary marks the title against two errors. It is not a badge of mere strangeness, as though Christians were called to be eccentric; the “peculiarity” is ownership—they belong wholly to God—and the fruit of that ownership is holiness and zeal for good works, not oddity. Nor is it a ground of pride, for they were called out of darkness by sovereign mercy and not for any worth of their own. To be a peculiar people is to be God's treasured possession, purchased by the blood of Christ, separated unto holiness, and existing to shew forth His praises.
webster_summary: The Authorized Version's title for God's redeemed as His own treasured possession (1 Peter 2:9); “peculiar” meaning belonging exclusively to God, the ground of holiness and zeal for good works, not of mere strangeness.
webster_full: PECULIAR PEOPLE, noun phrase. [Latin peculium, private property or treasure.] God's own treasured possession, His redeemed people.
Peter applies to the church the titles of Israel: a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a peculiar people (1 Peter 2:9).
Christ purifies unto Himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works (Titus 2:14).
Rooted at Sinai: a peculiar treasure above all people (Exodus 19:5).
The word means belonging wholly to God, not eccentric or merely odd.
scriptures: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Tit 2:14
Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.
For thou art an holy people unto the LORD thy God, and the LORD hath chosen thee to be a peculiar people unto himself, above all the nations that are upon the earth.
Now therefore, if ye will obey my voice indeed, and keep my covenant, then ye shall be a peculiar treasure unto me above all people: for all the earth is mine:
corruption_summary: The shifting of the English word from “treasured possession” to “strange” tempts believers to prize eccentricity for its own sake and to miss the ownership and holiness the title declares.
corruption_paragraphs: Because “peculiar” in modern English means odd or eccentric, the title is easily misread as a call to strangeness, as though the more curious and off-putting a Christian becomes, the more faithful he is. This is a corruption by linguistic drift. The biblical word means a treasured possession, that which belongs exclusively to its owner. The believer is peculiar because he is God's, bought with a price; the holiness that follows is the holiness of one set apart for the Master's use, not the affected oddity of one who confuses being disagreeable with being holy.

The opposite corruption empties the title of all distinctness, so that the people of God become indistinguishable from the world they were called out of. Peter holds both ends: they are called out of darkness into marvellous light, a holy nation set apart, and they are so that they should shew forth the praises of God in lives of zeal for good works. The dictionary recovers the title as the ground of grateful holiness: not strange for strangeness' sake, not worldly for ease's sake, but visibly and gladly the LORD's own treasure.
roots_summary: From the Latin peculium (private property), the Hebrew segullah (a treasured possession), and the Greek peripoiesis (a people for God's own possession); all naming exclusive ownership, not oddity.
roots_lines: Peculium, Latin, a man's private property or personal treasure, the root of “peculiar.”
Segullah, Hebrew, a special treasure or valued possession (Exodus 19:5).
Peripoiesis, Greek, a possession or acquisition, “a people for his own possession.”
Laos, Greek, a people, joined to the idea of belonging to God in 1 Peter 2:9.
The English sense shifted from “belonging exclusively to one” toward “strange,” obscuring the original.
usage: The pastor explained that “peculiar people” means God's treasured possession, not a license for eccentricity.
He reminded the church they were called out of darkness to shew forth God's praises, a holy nation set apart.
She found comfort that she was the LORD's peculiar treasure, purchased by the blood of Christ.

pos: noun (one who purifies metal; a title of God)
etymology: From the verb “refine,” through Old French refiner, to purify; rendering the Hebrew tsaraph, to smelt or refine metal, applied to God's purifying of His people.
biblical_def: A refiner is one who melts ore or metal in the fire to separate the precious from the dross, and Scripture takes up the image to teach how God purifies His people through affliction. Malachi foretells the coming of the LORD's messenger and asks, “Who may abide the day of his coming?… for he is like a refiner's fire”; and the LORD “shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver,” purging the sons of Levi as gold and silver that they may offer an offering in righteousness. Isaiah hears God say, “I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction.” The refiner's craft yields a rich theology of suffering: the fire is not destruction but purification; the dross is the sin and self that must be burned away; the heat is measured by the refiner's skill and watched until he sees his own image in the molten silver. So Peter writes that the trial of faith, more precious than gold, is tried with fire that it may be found unto praise and honour at the appearing of Jesus Christ. The dictionary marks the refiner against two errors: the prosperity gospel, which denies that God brings His people through the furnace at all, promising only ease; and the despairing heart, which reads affliction as the wrath of a judge rather than the skill of a Father. The Refiner sits—He does not abandon the crucible—and He brings forth His people as gold.
webster_summary: One who purifies metal in the fire; in Scripture a title of God, who sits as a refiner and purifier (Malachi 3:3), burning away the dross of His people through the furnace of affliction until His image appears.
webster_full: REFINER, noun. [Hebrew tsaraph, to smelt or refine.] One who melts metal in the fire to separate the precious from the dross.
A title of the LORD, who shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver (Malachi 3:3).
He is like a refiner's fire and fullers' soap, purging the sons of Levi.
He refines His people not with silver but in the furnace of affliction (Isaiah 48:10).
The trial of faith, tried with fire, is found unto praise at the appearing of Christ (1 Peter 1:7).
scriptures: Mal 3:3
And he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the LORD an offering in righteousness.
Mal 3:2
But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap:
Behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction.
That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ:
corruption_summary: The prosperity gospel denies the furnace altogether, while the despairing heart misreads it as the wrath of a judge; both miss the Refiner who sits over the crucible as a Father.
corruption_paragraphs: The prosperity gospel and the word-of-faith movement teach that the believer's portion is health, wealth, and ease, and that affliction is a sign of insufficient faith or hidden sin. The image of the Refiner overthrows this. God Himself says He chose His people in the furnace of affliction; the trial of faith, tried with fire, is the very means by which gold is proven. To promise a fireless faith is to promise what God has never promised and to leave the suffering saint to conclude he has failed when in truth he is being purified.

The opposite error is the despair that reads the furnace as the wrath of a judge bent on destruction. But the prophet does not say God burns His people up; He says God sits as a refiner and purifies them, watching the silver until His image appears, removing the dross, never the metal. The fire is measured by a Father's skill and love, ordered to a holy end—an offering in righteousness, a faith found unto praise. The dictionary recovers the Refiner: God does bring His people through the fire, and He never leaves the crucible until the work is done.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew tsaraph, to smelt, refine, or test metal in the fire; the refiner's craft of separating dross from silver becomes the figure of sanctifying affliction.
roots_lines: Tsaraph, Hebrew, to smelt, refine, or assay metal by fire.
Keseph, Hebrew, silver, the metal most often named in the refining image.
Kur, Hebrew, the smelting furnace, “the furnace of affliction” of Isaiah 48:10.
The Greek dokimion (1 Peter 1:7), the “trial” or proving of faith as gold is proved.
The dross (Hebrew sig) figures the sin and self the fire burns away.
usage: In the sickroom the pastor read Malachi and reminded the sufferer that the Refiner sits, and does not leave the crucible.
He warned against the prosperity gospel, for God chose His people in the furnace of affliction, not apart from it.
She learned to read her trial as the refiner's fire, ordered by a Father until His image appeared in her.
